segs.text:
GUIDE TO THE JEWISH YEAR
ELUL
1 Beginning on the first day of Elul (the second day of Rosh Ḥodesh) and for the entire month of Elul, it is customary to say לְְדָוִד, יהוה אוֹרִי (page 193) in the evening at the end of Ma’ariv and in the morning after saying the Psalm of the Day [אשי ישראל, פמ"ה: ג].

segs.en: Shofar blasts in Elul
segs.text: 2 In addition, four shofar blasts are sounded at the end of weekday morning prayers, prior to (or following) recitation of לְְדָוִד, יהוה אוֹרִי [רמ"א או"ח, תקפא: א].

segs.en: Changes to Kaddish on Rosh HaShana
segs.text: 13 Changes to the Kaddish: It is customary to replace the phrase לְְעֵֽלָּא מִן כָָּל (“beyond any”) with לְְעֵֽלָּא לְְעֵֽלָּא מִכָָּל (“above and beyond any”) [משנ"ב, נו: ב] and to change the phrase עֹשֶׂה שָׁלוֹם (“He who makes peace”) to עֹשֶׂה הַשָּׁלוֹם (“He who makes the peace”) [ערוה"ש או"ח, תקפב: ח]. segs.en: Number and timing of shofar blasts
segs.text: 24 The first thirty shofar blasts sounded prior to Musaf represent the minimum number of shofar sounds that one is required to hear [שו"ע או"ח, תקצ: א]. However, it is customary to blow a hundred blasts. The Ashkenazi custom is to blow thirty before Musaf, thirty during the Repetition of the Amida and forty more in sets of thirty and ten during the Full Kaddish after Musaf [משנ"ב, תקצב: ד]. Some congregations follow the Sephardi custom of blowing the shofar during the silent Amida, rather than the Repetition (see law 34).

segs.en: Posture during shofar blowing
segs.text: 25 The person blowing the shofar is required to stand; the congregation is permitted to sit during the first set of shofar sounds, although the custom is to stand [שו"ע או"ח, תקפה: א; משנ"ב, שם: ב].

segs.en: Blessings for shofar blowing
segs.text: 26 Two blessings are said by the person blowing the shofar: (1) לִשְְְׁמֹֽעַ קוֹל שׁוֹפָר, and (2) שֶׁהֶחֱיָֽנוּ [שו"ע או"ח, תקפה: ב].

segs.en: Restrictions on speech during shofar blowing
segs.text: 27 To prevent distractions while performing the mitzva of hearing the shofar, the congregation is, until completion of the first thirty shofar blasts, forbidden to speak about matters unrelated to shofar and, until completion of the hundredth blast, forbidden to speak about matters unrelated to prayer [שו"ע או"ח, תקצב: ג].

segs.en: Prohibition of shofar on Shabbat
segs.text: 28 The rabbis ruled that we do not blow the shofar when Rosh HaShana falls on Shabbat [ראש השנה, כט:; שו"ע או"ח, תקפח: ה].

segs.en: Musaf for Rosh HaShana: nine blessings
segs.text: 30 Musaf for Rosh HaShana: Unique among the Amidot said on Shabbat and Yom Tov, the Musaf for Rosh HaShana comprises nine blessings, rather than seven. Instead of one blessing devoted to the Festival, there are three extended blessings dedicated to three separate Rosh HaShana themes: Kingship, Remembrance and the Shofar [שו"ע או"ח, תקצא: א; שם: ד].

segs.text: 47 The fast begins at dawn [שו"ע או"ח, תקנ: ב]. One is permitted to wake before dawn to eat and drink, but only if one had the intention to do so before going to sleep [שו"ע או"ח, תקסד: א].

parts.en: Laws of Mashiv HaRuach
One begins saying Mashiv HaRuach in Musaf of Shemini Atzeret and continues until Musaf of the first day of Pesach

segs.en: If one forgets to say Mashiv HaRuach in its proper place but realizes before beginning the words of the blessing Mechayeh HaMetim, one should immediately say Mashiv HaRuach and continue with the rest of the blessing. If one realizes the omission immediately after completing the blessing Mechayeh HaMetim, one should say Mashiv HaRuach and continue with the following blessing. If one realizes the omission after beginning the words Atah Kadosh, one must repeat the Amida from the beginning.
segs.text: 130 If one forgets to say מַשִּׁיב הָרֽוּחַ in its proper place but realizes before beginning the words of the blessing מְְחַיֵּה הַמֵּתִים, one should immediately say מַשִּׁיב הָרֽוּחַ and continue with the rest of the blessing. If one realizes the omission immediately after completing the blessing מְְחַיֵּה הַמֵּתִים, one should say מַשִּׁיב הָרֽוּחַ and continue with the following blessing. If one realizes the omission after beginning the words אַתָּה קָדוֹשׁ, one must repeat the Amida from the beginning [שו"ע או"ח, קיד: ו].

parts.en: Torah Reading: pages 1161–1167. The Torah reading is repeated, in cycles of five aliyot, until all males over thirteen have received an aliya [Rema Orach Chaim 697:1]. It is customary for children under 13 years to participate in an aliya, known as Kol HaNe'arim, in which multiple tallitot are spread to form a canopy over the children and the oleh. This is followed by the calling up of the Chatan Torah, for whom the final verses of the Torah are read. After the completion of the reading, it is customary that Hagbaha is performed with arms crossed, so that when the Torah is raised and the arms uncrossed, the lettering on the scroll faces outward toward the congregation. A second scroll is opened; the Chatan Bereshit is called up and the first verses of Bereshit are read [Shulchan Aruch and Rema Orach Chaim 697:1]. It is customary to pause in the reading for the congregation to read aloud Veyehi-Erev Veyehi Voker for each day of Creation, and to read aloud the last three verses, starting with Veyechulu HaShamayim. This is followed by Half Kaddish. A third scroll is opened for Maftir. The Haftara is the beginning of the book of Joshua (page 1166) [ibid].

segs.text: 148 If one forgets to say וְְתֵן טַל וּמָטָר לִבְְְרָכָה in its proper place but realizes before saying God’s name in the ninth blessing (מְְבָרֵךְְְ הַשָּׁנִים), one should immediately say וְְתֵן טַל וּמָטָר לִבְְְרָכָה and continue with the rest of the blessing. If one realizes the omission after completing the blessing מְְבָרֵךְְְ הַשָּׁנִים, one should say וְְתֵן טַל וּמָטָר לִבְְְרָכָה prior to the words כִּי אַתָּה שׁוֹמֵֽעַ in the sixteenth blessing (שׁוֹמֵֽעַ תְְּפִלָּה). If one realizes the omission after beginning the seventeenth blessing (רְְצֵה), one must repeat the Amida from the beginning of the ninth blessing (מְְבָרֵךְְְ הַשָּׁנִים). If one realizes the omission after completing the Amida, one must repeat the entire Amida [שו"ע או"ח, קיז: ה].

After thirty days, one should assume that one said וְְתֵן טַל וּמָטָר לִבְְְרָכָה.

segs.text: 151 It is customary to light Ḥanukka lights in the synagogue, either before or after Ma’ariv of each evening of Ḥanukka. The procedure is identical to that of lighting in the home, as described below, except that the lights should be placed along the southern wall of the synagogue.

152 After Ma’ariv, Ḥanukka lights are lit in the home. On the first night, three blessings are said: (1) לְְהַדְְְלִיק נֵר שֶׁל חֲנֻכָּה, (2) שֶׁעָשָׂה נִסִּים (“Who performed miracles”) and (3) שֶׁהֶחֱיָֽנוּ (page 897). On subsequent nights, only the first two blessings are said [שו"ע או"ח, תרעו: א]. When adding lights each night, the new light is always added to the left. The newest candle is lit first, and one then lights the rest of the lights from left to right.

153 The lights must burn for at least half an hour after nightfall [שו"ע או"ח, תרעב: ב; משנ"ב, שם: ד]. If one did not light during this time, one is permitted to light any time before daybreak. In such a case, one says the appropriate blessings when lighting, but only if other household members are awake [שו"ע, שם; משנ"ב, שם: יא].
154 Most have the custom for each member of the household to light separately, but the head of household may light one menora for the entire family [ שו"ע ורמ"א או"ח, תרעא: ב].

155 KislevWomen are obligated to light Ḥanukka lights [שו"ע או"ח, תרעה: ג]. Hence, a woman can light for herself, on behalf of her household, and on behalf of an adult male [משנ"ב, שם: ט].Guide to the Jewish year
156 The menora is generally lit indoors, but near a window, so that the lights are visible to the general public as well [שו"ע או"ח, תרעה: ז].
157 After the lighting, it is customary to sing הַנֵּרוֹת הַלָּֽלוּ and מָעוֹז צוּר (pages 899–901) [שו"ע או"ח, תרעו: ד].

parts.text: 201 As soon as possible after dark,

parts.en: Bedikat Chametz

in one's home (page 759) [Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 441:1]. It is customary for a household member to hide ten pieces of chametz to be found during the search [Rema Orach Chaim 442:2]. Before beginning the search one says the blessing Al Bedikat Chametz [Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 442:1]. The custom is to conduct the search at night by the light of a candle, but use of a flashlight is also permitted. If Pesach falls on Motzaei Shabbat, the search is made on Thursday night. Those who plan to be away on Pesach should conduct the search the night before their departure, but without making a blessing. After completion of the search, one says Kol Chamira (page 759), an Aramaic formula disclaiming one's ownership of any chametz the whereabouts of which are unknown.

segs.en: First Evening of Chol HaMoed: Maariv for weekdays (page 243) is said. In the fourth blessing of the Amida, the paragraph of Atah Chonen (page 261) is said. In the ninth blessing of the Amida (Birkat HaShanim), one begins to say Veten Beracha, a practice which will continue until December 4th (or, in some years, December 5th) (see law 147). If one erroneously says Veten Tal U'Matar LeVracha in the spring and summer months, one must repeat the Amida. If one realizes the error before completing the Amida, one must repeat the Amida from the beginning of Birkat HaShanim [Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim 117:3]. In the seventeenth blessing of the Amida (Retzei), Ya'aleh VeYavo is added.
segs.text: 227 First Evening of Ḥol HaMo’ed: Ma’ariv for weekdays (page 243) is said. In the fourth blessing of the Amida, the paragraph of אַתָּה חוֹנַנְְְתָּֽנוּ (page 261) is said. If one realizes the error before completing the Amida, one must repeat the Amida from the beginning of ברכת השנים[שו”ע או”ח, קיז: ג]. In the seventeenth blessing of the Amida (רְְצֵה), יַעֲלֶה וְְיָבוֹא is added.

During the period of counting the Omer, certain mourning rituals are observed: one does not cut one's hair, shave, listen to music, or hold weddings and other parties. Some permit shaving during this period. These practices commemorate a plague that killed twelve thousand pairs of students of Rabbi Akiva who, the Talmud says, did not honor one another properly. The Ashkenazi community intensified these mourning customs in the wake of the pogroms of the First Crusade, which took place in Iyar and Sivan in the year 1096 (4856).

This day commemorates the Jews who gave their lives in defense of the Jewish settlement in the land of Israel, including soldiers of the Israel Defense Forces killed in the line of duty and civilians murdered in acts of terror. On Yom HaZikaron eve, a yahrzeit candle is lit and the Mourner's Kaddish is said by a bereaved parent, spouse or child. At the end of Shacharit, some congregations say special prayers.

parts.en: Ma'ariv: Customs differ. The service adopted by the Israeli Chief Rabbinate is as follows: selections from Psalms and other readings precede Ma'ariv for weekdays. It is customary for the Shaliaḥ Tzibbur to lead Ma'ariv using melodies associated with Yom Tov. After the Amida, the Shaliaḥ Tzibbur says Full Kaddish. Responsive readings and Psalm 126 to the tune of 'HaTikva' follow. The service concludes with the counting of the Omer, Aleinu, Mourner's Kaddish and communal singing of Ani Ma'amin.

parts.en: Shacharit: Pesukei DeZimra as for Shabbat and Yom Tov, with the addition of Mizmor LeTodah. Nishmat is not said. After Az Yashir, prayers continue with Shacharit for weekdays. The Repetition of the Amida by the Shaliaḥ Tzibbur is followed by Hallel and Half Kaddish. On a Thursday the Torah is taken from the Ark and the appropriate section of the Torah is read. After the Torah reading, Half Kaddish is said. Haftara is said without blessings. The Prayer for the State of Israel is said, followed by the Memorial Prayer for fallen soldiers. Shacharit continues as for weekdays. At the end of the service, the congregation sings Ani Ma'amin.

Ashrei and Uva LeTziyon are said, followed by Full Kaddish, Aleinu, Mourner's Kaddish, the Daily Psalm, and Mourner's Kaddish.

segs.en: Candle lighting: Two blessings are said: (1) 'To kindle the candle of the Festival', and (2) Shehecheyanu. On Friday night, the conclusion of the first blessing is: 'To kindle the candle of Shabbat and the Festival'.
segs.text: 276 Candle lighting: Two blessings are said: (1) לְְהַדְְְלִיק נֵר שֶׁל יוֹם טוֹב, and (2) שֶׁהֶחֱיָֽנוּ. On Friday night, the conclusion of the first blessing is: לְְהַדְְְלִיק נֵר שֶׁל שַׁבָּת וְְשֶׁל יוֹם טוֹב.

parts.en: Ma'ariv: for Shabbat and Yom Tov. The custom is to begin Ma'ariv after nightfall. Many congregations say the special verse for Yom Tov (Vayidaber Moshe), before saying the Amida for Yom Tov. This is followed by Full Kaddish, Aleinu and Mourner's Kaddish. It is customary to conclude with the singing of Adon Olam or Yigdal.

parts.en: When Shavuot eve falls on Friday night, Ma'ariv is preceded by the last two psalms of Kabbalat Shabbat: Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbat and Adonai Malach. Bameh Madlikin is omitted. VeShamru and the special verse for Yom Tov (Vayidaber Moshe) precede the Yom Tov Amida, which is said with additions for Shabbat. After the Amida, the congregation says Vayechulu, and the Shaliaḥ Tzibbur says the abbreviated Repetition of the Amida as is customary on Shabbat eve. When Shavuot eve falls on Motza'ei Shabbat, the congregation adds the paragraph Vatodi'enu in the middle section of the Amida. Similarly, in Kiddush, the two blessings for Havdala are inserted prior to the blessing Shehecheyanu; thus the order of blessings is: wine, Kiddush, flame, Havdala, Shehecheyanu.

Shacharit: for Shabbat and Yom Tov. The Shaliaḥ Tzibbur for Shacharit begins from the words Ha'el Betatzumot Ozcha. After Barekhu, the congregation says HaMeir La'aretz or, if it is also Shabbat, Hakol Yoducha. The Amida for Yom Tov is said; if also Shabbat, one says the additions for Shabbat. The Repetition of the Amida is followed by Hallel and Full Kaddish. On the second day of Shavuot, Megillat Rut is read, followed by Mourner's Kaddish.

parts.en: Torah Reading: first day – page 1146; second day – page 1143. Five men are called up, seven on Shabbat. Many congregations stand during the reading of the Ten Commandments. Maftir (both days): page 1149. Haftara: first day – page 1149; second day – page 1151. By custom, an Aramaic poem, Yatziv P'tagum, is said after the first two verses of the Haftara of the second day.

parts.en: According to the Mishna (Ta'anit 4:6), the fast of the 17th of Tammuz commemorates five calamities that befell the Jewish people on that date: (1) Moses broke the tablets, (2) the daily Tamid sacrifice was interrupted (in Second Temple times), (3) the walls of Jerusalem were breached by Titus, (4) Apostemus burned the Torah, and (5) an idol was introduced to the Temple.

parts.en: During the silent Amida, those who are fasting say Aneinu as part of the sixteenth blessing, Shomea Tefilla. During the Repetition of the Amida, the Shaliaḥ Tzibbur says Aneinu between the seventh and eighth blessings, as in the morning. After the eighteenth blessing (Modim), the Shaliaḥ Tzibbur says the paragraph relating to Birkat Kohanim. For the final blessing of the Amida, Sim Shalom is said instead of Shalom Rav. After the Amida, the congregation says Avinu Malkenu. This is followed by Tachanun, Full Kaddish and Aleinu.

parts.en: Shabbat Chazon (Shabbat preceding Tisha B'Av). The Shabbat preceding Tisha B'Av is known as Shabbat Chazon, named for the first word of the Haftara, Chazon. On Friday night, many congregations sing Lekha Dodi to the melody of Eli Tzion. The special Haftara (Is. 1:1–27) is read to the tune of Eikha.

parts.en: Tisha B'Av (9th of Av). According to the Mishna (Ta'anit 4:6), the fast of the 9th of Av commemorates five calamities that befell the Jewish people on that date: (1) God decreed that the children of Israel would not be allowed to enter the land of Israel, (2) the First Temple was destroyed, (3) the Second Temple was destroyed, (4) Beitar was captured, and (5) Jerusalem was plowed over.

The fast begins at sunset. In addition to eating and drinking, one is prohibited from washing and anointing oneself and from wearing leather shoes. Marital relations are likewise forbidden. One abstains from Torah study, except for topics such as mourning laws, Eikha, Job, and the unhappy portions of Jeremiah. One does not greet other people or inquire after their welfare.

Mincha ends with Full Kaddish and Aleinu.

parts.en: Tu B'Av (15th of Av). According to the Mishna (Ta'anit 4:8), on the 15th of Av, the young women of Jerusalem would put on borrowed white dresses and dance together in the vineyards. Young men would come out to watch them, and the women would urge the men not to be swayed by beauty, but to be drawn to women of good family.
